answer.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure to answer with promotional_pricing, but memory_73 is the one inherited record with a quantified downstream cost: +31% signup and +18% revenue bought at -12pp monthly retention. That is a near-term-lift/late-harm signature, and it argues directly against discounting under a 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective. It is also the terse, heavily compressed entry ('segment def unchanged' is an unexplained caveat), so it is worth one verification pull to confirm whether the retention loss was measured over enough months and whether the segment definition drifted. The two real declines are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so fixing it plausibly moves both; memory_86 and memory_31 both point that way and memory_91 (activation messaging) is the narrower downstream lever. I spend the second pull on memory_86 because it is the direct basis for the action I intend and because, as summarized, it reports only early-funnel outcomes (completion, time-to-value, early adoption) with no retention or revenue-quality readout. That is the same shape of evidence that made the discount look good at first. Key uncertainty I am not resolving away: 'shorter onboarding' can improve completion by removing steps that were qualifying or value-establishing, producing more accounts of lower quality; the inherited summaries cannot rule this out. So I will run it as a standard experiment with explicit downstream guardrails - 60-90 day retention, paid-conversion rate, and qualified-revenue-per-signup measured against a holdout - rather than treating memory_86 as settled. If verification shows memory_86's original record also lacked downstream measurement, I will shrink to a small guarded test rather than escalate scale.
